Infinity-harmonic functions in the plane:
Regularity by injectivity

Karl K. Brustad. August 24, 2026 Email: karl.brustad@momentumtechnologies.com Address: Momentum Technologies
Ranheimsveien 9
7044 Trondheim
Norway
Abstract

It has been a long standing conjecture that the ∞\infty-harmonic functions in the plane have a 1/3-Hölder continuous gradient. It is known that solutions are C1C^{1} and that the gradient is locally α\alpha-Hölder, but α\alpha comes without any positive lower bound. Aronsson’s solution x4/3−y4/3x^{4/3}-y^{4/3} shows that no better general regularity is possible.

In the plane there is also a connection between the ∞\infty-Laplace equation and the one-dimensional heat equation, observed already by Aronsson himself. I shall show that this link can be accessed under a certain injectivity condition on the gradient, and that the caloric structure then is enough to prove the 1/3-Hölder continuity. Of course, an injective gradient is by no means a necessary condition, as seen by smooth solutions such as the planes and cones.

1 Introduction

A function u:Ω→ℝu\colon\Omega\to\mathbb{R} is said to be ∞\infty-harmonic in Ω⊆ℝn\Omega\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{n} if

Δ∞​u=0\Delta_{\infty}u=0

in the viscosity sense. The ∞\infty-Laplace operator is Δ∞u:=∇uℋu∇u⊤\Delta_{\infty}u:=\nabla u\mathcal{H}u\nabla u^{\top} where ∇u=[ux1,…,uxn]:Ω→ℝn\nabla u=[u_{x_{1}},\dots,u_{x_{n}}]\colon\Omega\to\mathbb{R}^{n} is the gradient and where ℋ​u=[uxi,xj]i,j=1n:Ω→ℝn×n\mathcal{H}u=\left[u_{x_{i},x_{j}}\right]_{i,j=1}^{n}\colon\Omega\to\mathbb{R}^{n\times n} is the Hessian matrix of uu. In the plane the equation reads

ux2​ux​x+2​ux​uy​ux​y+uy2​uy​y=0.u_{x}^{2}u_{xx}+2u_{x}u_{y}u_{xy}+u_{y}^{2}u_{yy}=0.
Theorem 1.1.

Suppose uu is ∞\infty-harmonic in an open Ω⊆ℝ2\Omega\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{2} with ∇u≠0\nabla u\neq 0.

If

|∇u(x)−∇u(y)|≥C1|x−y|,C1>0,x,y∈Ω,|\nabla u(x)-\nabla u(y)|\geq C_{1}|x-y|,\qquad C_{1}>0,\;x,y\in\Omega, (1.1)

then, locally in Ω\Omega, there is a constant C2>0C_{2}>0 such that

|∇u​(x)−∇u​(y)|≤C2​|x−y|1/3.|\nabla u(x)-\nabla u(y)|\leq C_{2}|x-y|^{1/3}. (1.2)

The condition (1.1) – sometimes called metric injectivity – clearly implies that the gradient ∇u:Ω→ℝ2\nabla u\colon\Omega\to\mathbb{R}^{2} is 1-1 onto B:=∇u​(Ω)B:=\nabla u(\Omega), with a C1−1C_{1}^{-1}-Lipschitz inverse 𝐟:B→Ω\mathbf{f}\colon B\to\Omega.

Remark 1.1.

It is an interesting question whether the caloric realm can be accessed also with (1.1) weakened to a mere injectivity of the gradient. I think it probably does, but the proof will require better versions of Lemma 2.1 and Proposition 2.1.

Remark 1.2.

This paper is limited to the situation ∇u≠0\nabla u\neq 0. It is perhaps possible to also include critical points, but, as we shall see, it would then be necessary to analyse the behaviour of the associated caloric functions in the limit t→∞t\to\infty.

Lemma 2.1.

A Lipschitz inverse 𝐟\mathbf{f} of a continuous gradient field ∇u\nabla u is again a gradient field. A potential w∈C1,1w\in C^{1,1} is given by

w⁡(p):=p⊤​𝐟​(p)−u⁡(𝐟⁡(p)).w(p):=p^{\top}\mathbf{f}(p)-u(\mathbf{f}(p)). (2.1)

Note that the result is immediate if 𝐟\mathbf{f} is differentiable with Jacobian matrix ∇𝐟\nabla\mathbf{f}. Because then

∇w(p)=𝐟⊤(p)+p⊤∇𝐟(p)−∇u(𝐟(p))∇𝐟(p)=𝐟⊤(p),\nabla w(p)=\mathbf{f}^{\top}(p)+p^{\top}\nabla\mathbf{f}(p)-\nabla u(\mathbf{f}(p))\nabla\mathbf{f}(p)=\mathbf{f}^{\top}(p),

since ∇u​(𝐟​(p))=p⊤\nabla u(\mathbf{f}(p))=p^{\top}.

|∇u​(x)−∇u​(y)||x−y|1/3\displaystyle\frac{\left|\nabla u(x)-\nabla u(y)\right|}{\left|x-y\right|^{1/3}} =|p−q||𝐟⁡(p)−𝐟⁡(q)|1/3\displaystyle=\frac{\left|p-q\right|}{\left|\mathbf{f}(p)-\mathbf{f}(q)\right|^{1/3}}

≤1C1/3.\displaystyle\leq\frac{1}{C^{1/3}}.

This completes the proof of the Theorem.

3 Examples

3.1 The ∞\infty-potential in the square

In [Bru26] it is shown that the (unique viscosity) solution of the Dirichlet problem

{Δ∞​u=0in Ω∖{(1,1)},u=0on ∂Ω,u=1at (1,1),\begin{cases}\Delta_{\infty}u=0\qquad&\text{in $\Omega\setminus\{(1,1)\}$},\\ u=0&\text{on $\partial\Omega$,}\\ u=1&\text{at $(1,1)$,}\end{cases} (3.1)

in the square Ω={(x,y)| 0<x<2, 0<y<2}\Omega=\{(x,y)\;|\;0<x<2,\,0<y<2\} has an invertible gradient in the sub-square Ω1={(x,y)| 0<x<1, 0<y<1}\Omega_{1}=\{(x,y)\;|\;0<x<1,\,0<y<1\}. Here, B1:=∇u(Ω1)={(p,q)| 0<p2+q2<1,p>0,q>0}B_{1}:=\nabla u(\Omega_{1})=\left\{(p,q)\,|\,0<p^{2}+q^{2}<1,\;p>0,\,q>0\right\} and the potential w⁡(p)=p⊤​𝐟​(p)−u⁡(𝐟⁡(p))w(p)=p^{\top}\mathbf{f}(p)-u(\mathbf{f}(p)) of the inverse 𝐟:B1→Ω1\mathbf{f}\colon B_{1}\to\Omega_{1} in (ψ,t)(\psi,t)-coordinates is shown to be the caloric function

h⁡(ψ,t)=8π​(e−4​t6​sin⁡(2​ψ)+e−36​t210​sin⁡(6​ψ)+e−100​t990​sin⁡(10​ψ)+⋯)h(\psi,t)=\frac{8}{\pi}\left(\frac{e^{-4t}}{6}\sin(2\psi)+\frac{e^{-36t}}{210}\sin(6\psi)+\frac{e^{-100t}}{990}\sin(10\psi)+\cdots\right) (3.2)

in D={(ψ,t)| 0<ψ⁡<π2,t>​0}D=\left\{(\psi,t)\,|\,0<\psi<\frac{\pi}{2},\;t>0\right\}. Moreover, for v=−h−htv=-h-h_{t},

vψ​(ψ,t)=−4π​ϑ​(2​ψ,e−16​t)v_{\psi}(\psi,t)=-\frac{4}{\pi}\vartheta(2\psi,e^{-16t})

where ϑ\vartheta is the second Jacobi Theta function. Also, vψv_{\psi} is zero in DD exactly when ψ=π/4\psi=\pi/4, which corresponds to the diagonal in Ω1\Omega_{1}.

Since 𝐟\mathbf{f} is real-analytic it is locally Lipschitz, which in turn implies the condition (1.1) locally on ∇u\nabla u. We therefore have the following Corollary to the Theorem.

Corollary 3.1.

The ∞\infty-potential in the square is Cl​o​c1,13.C_{loc}^{1,\frac{1}{3}}.

More specifically, the gradient is (at least) Lipschitz near the medians (xx or y=1y=1), it is (exactly) C1/3C^{1/3} near the diagonals, and real-analytic elsewhere.

For u⁡(x,y)=34​(x4/3−y4/3)u(x,y)=\frac{3}{4}\left(x^{4/3}-y^{4/3}\right),

[p,q]=∇u​(x,y)=[x1/3,−y1/3].[p,q]=\nabla u(x,y)=[x^{1/3},-y^{1/3}].

Appendix A
Proof of Lemma 2.2

I explicitly state the key property needed for the proof of Lemma 2.2.

Lemma A.1.

Let Ω⊆ℝn\Omega\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{n}, n≥2n\geq 2, be open and assume that u∈C1​(Ω)u\in C^{1}(\Omega) is ∞\infty-subharmonic in Ω\Omega. i.e., Δ∞​u≥0\Delta_{\infty}u\geq 0 in the viscosity sense.

Let x0∈Ωx_{0}\in\Omega and let 0<r<dist⁡(x0,∂Ω)0<r<\dist(x_{0},\partial\Omega). If x∈∂Br​(x0)x\in\partial B_{r}(x_{0}) satisfies

u⁡(x)=max|z−x0|≤r⁡u⁡(z)=max|z−x0|=r⁡u⁡(z),u(x)=\max_{|z-x_{0}|\leq r}u(z)=\max_{|z-x_{0}|=r}u(z),

then

|∇u​(x0)|≤u⁡(x)−u⁡(x0)r≤|∇u​(x)|.|\nabla u(x_{0})|\leq\frac{u(x)-u(x_{0})}{r}\leq|\nabla u(x)|.
Proof.

This is Lemma 4.1(d) together with Lemma 4.3 in [Cra08]. ∎

Proof of Lemma 2.2.

I mimic the proof of Proposition 6.2 in [Cra08]. The idea is to construct a sequence (γk)k(\gamma_{k})_{k} of curves γk:[0,Tk]→V\gamma_{k}:[0,T_{k}]\to V, and show that a limit curve γ\gamma has the desired properties.

For a fixed small δ>0\delta>0 let [x0,x1,…,xJ][x^{0},x^{1},\dots,x^{J}] be a list of points in VV defined recursively as x0=xx^{0}=x, and with xj+1x^{j+1} chosen so that

This is when dist⁡(xj,∂V)>δ\dist(x^{j},\partial V)>\delta. If dist⁡(xj,∂V)≤δ\dist(x^{j},\partial V)\leq\delta we stop and set J:=jJ:=j and T:=J​δT:=J\delta. We have by Lemma A.1 that
